evaluated.name: Externally_Financed_Tangible_Buildout
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 1), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(xrd, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Raising external debt and equity to fund expansion is most value-destructive at intangible-poor firms, which lack the knowledge assets needed to earn a spread over the cost of the new capital.
evaluated.reasoning: The external-financing anomaly and the intangible-intensity premium point in opposite directions, so their interaction should sharpen both: capital raised by intangible-lean, commodity-like producers is the clearest case of overinvestment. Conditioning the financing measure on low intangible intensity makes the mechanism about who is raising the money, not merely how much.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Growth_With_Weak_Intangible_Productivity
evaluated.hypothesis: Asset growth predicts low returns mainly when the existing capital base, measured inclusive of recognized intangibles, is already generating little revenue per dollar deployed; growth by capital-efficient firms is a positive-NPV signal instead.
evaluated.reasoning: Sales per unit of combined tangible and intangible capital is a direct measure of whether prior investment has been converted into output, so it identifies which growers are compounding an unproductive asset base. The interaction conditions the classic investment effect on intangible-inclusive capital productivity rather than treating all growth identically.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Knowledge_Pivot_Capex_Retrenchment
evaluated.hypothesis: A cut in the physical investment rate carries very different information depending on where the firm's productive capacity resides: for R&D-intensive firms it signals a deliberate pivot toward knowledge production (asset-light, high expected returns on expensed intangible capital), whereas for tangible-capital firms it is closer to ordinary capacity contraction.
evaluated.reasoning: The expression is multiplicative rather than additive, so it only lights up when a high R&D-to-assets firm simultaneously reduces its capex-to-PP&E rate, which is exactly the conditional claim rather than a sum of the R&D premium and the investment-decline effect. Scaling capex by the installed PP&E base and taking its first difference removes the mechanical "ratio rises because capex fell" artifact of the earlier mix variable, and using reported xrd (no zero-fill) prevents a large point mass at zero from destroying cross-sectional discrimination, at the cost of restricting the sample to firms for which the knowledge-pivot mechanism is even defined.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Plant_Buildout_Without_Knowledge_Capital
evaluated.hypothesis: The return penalty on gross plant expansion is concentrated among firms with essentially no accumulated knowledge capital, because capacity added without proprietary technology competes away its own rents; the same expansion by research-rich firms complements existing intangible capital and is not penalized.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the rank difference with a rank product makes the signal extreme only in the joint corner (fast PP&E growth AND a thin five-year R&D stock), which is the interaction the hypothesis asserts and which cannot be produced by stacking the PP&E-growth and R&D-intensity anomalies. Cumulating R&D over five years and scaling by sales measures the depth of the knowledge moat rather than one year of spending, and zero-filling is economically appropriate here because genuinely non-innovating firms are the intended conditioning group.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Acquisitions_By_Non_Innovators
evaluated.hypothesis: Acquisition-driven growth destroys value mainly when the acquirer has no internal research capability: such firms buy growth options at a competitive control premium precisely because they cannot build them, and they lack the absorptive capacity to integrate acquired technology.
evaluated.reasoning: The multiplicative form tests whether acquirer underperformance is state-dependent on the buyer's own knowledge stock, rather than blending two standalone anomalies with a rank difference; a research-intensive serial acquirer and a research-barren one receive very different scores at identical acquisition intensity. It is also mechanically distinct from the accepted goodwill signal, which keys on total asset growth financed by goodwill additions rather than on cash acquisition intensity conditioned on absent internal R&D.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Acquired_Growth_Without_Organic_Revenue
evaluated.hypothesis: Buying growth is value-destructive precisely when the firm's own top line is stalling: managers of decelerating businesses overpay for targets, and the purchase premium booked as goodwill is later impaired.
evaluated.reasoning: Gen-0's acquisition signal delivered a big alpha but a −0.8 FMB t-stat because its conditioner (five-year R&D/sales) is essentially an industry dummy with a mass point at zero; replacing it with firm-level organic revenue growth gives a continuous, firm-specific measure of *why* the firm is acquiring. Combining cash acquisition spend with the contemporaneous goodwill addition captures both the outlay and the unidentifiable-intangible premium in a single scaled flow.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hiring_Binge_Low_RD_Per_Worker
evaluated.hypothesis: Rapid headcount expansion is a negative-return investment signal when each worker is backed by little research spending, because such labor is a low-skill fixed cost added at the cycle peak; at knowledge-intensive firms new hires embody intangible capital formation.
evaluated.reasoning: This opens a distinct economic channel — labor as an investment margin — and R&D per employee is a firm-specific knowledge-intensity measure that is far less collinear with industry membership than R&D/sales. Employment growth is also nearly orthogonal to the CMA construction, so any alpha here is less likely to be absorbed by FF5.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex_Commitment_With_Bloating_Knowledge_Capital
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm's stock of knowledge and recognized intangible capital keeps growing relative to the revenue it generates, the intangible base is failing to convert into sales; continuing to commit physical capital on top of that unproductive intangible base is overinvestment and is followed by low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The mechanical coupling the critic flagged is removed because the investment leg (capx over installed PP&E) shares no variable with the conditioner, whose denominator is revenue rather than a capital base that capex inflates. It also changes the economic object from a static productivity level (the archive signal) to a multi-year deterioration in the revenue yield of intangible capital, and dividing by revt rather than by a possibly-zero intangible stock keeps the ratio well defined for the broad sample.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex_Push_Amid_Research_Retrenchment
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that is simultaneously ramping physical spending and cutting its smoothed research budget is harvesting a maturing franchise: the visible capex is read as growth by investors while the quiet research cut reveals that the underlying product pipeline is being wound down.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are now firm-level flow growth rates with no sales scaling, eliminating the "ratio moves because the denominator moved" artifact in the previous conditioner. Dropping COALESCE removes the degenerate mass of exactly-zero deltas at non-reporting firms, so the interaction is estimated only where a research-retrenchment decision actually exists, and smoothing R&D over three years ensures the cut reflects strategy rather than a one-year timing blip.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity_Expansion_Into_Eroding_Rents
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross margin is the realized cash return on a firm's intangible assets — brand, technology, and customer franchise — so a multi-year margin slide means those rents are eroding; firms that expand physical capacity into an eroding franchise are adding capacity to a commoditizing business and earn low subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the industry-neutralization robustness exercise with a different economic channel: the conditioner is the *realized output* of intangible capital rather than another measure of intangible input spending, so it is not a restatement of the archive's R&D-intensity leg. Because sale and cogs are near-universally reported, the conditioner has no zero mass point and full coverage, and its trend form captures franchise decay rather than a single noisy year.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Acquired_Intangible_Heavy_Base_Low_Gross_Profitability
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0)), ADD(ppent, ADD(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A capital base dominated by purchased intangibles and goodwill rather than productive plant is only justified if those intangibles generate gross profit; when gross profitability is low, the carrying value is impairment-prone and the firm's past acquisition-driven investment was value-destroying, predicting low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The previous share collapsed to 1.0 for every non-R&D reporter, but this composition measure uses balance-sheet stocks whose denominator always contains PP&E, so it is continuous and defined across the whole sample rather than acting as a reporting dummy. The mechanism is also different from the archive's financing and acquisition-flow signals: it asks whether the *accumulated* mix of purchased intangible versus physical capital is being validated by gross profit, making impairment risk, not current investment intensity, the source of predictability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory_Buildup_Without_Pricing_Power
evaluated.hypothesis: Inventory accumulation is an investment decision whose payoff depends on brand and product differentiation: a commodity producer with no gross-margin cushion that builds stock is producing goods it will have to discount, whereas a high-margin, brand-supported firm can carry inventory profitably.
evaluated.reasoning: This opens the working-capital investment margin, which is untouched by the archive and largely orthogonal to CMA's asset-growth construction, while retaining the level gross-margin conditioner that has been the archive's most reliable intangible leg. Coverage is essentially full because inventory, sales, and cost of goods are near-universally reported, avoiding the zero-mass problem that has broken the FMB slopes of the R&D-conditioned signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Physical_Investment_With_RD_At_Own_History_Low
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms that actually run research programs, pushing physical capital while research spending sits at the bottom of its own five-year range signals a deliberate wind-down of the innovation pipeline in favor of harvesting existing capacity, and such firms subsequently underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the diagnosis of `Capex_Push_Amid_Research_Retrenchment`, whose −5.1% alpha coexisted with a null FMB slope: replacing an unbounded growth rate with a bounded position-in-own-history statistic removes the tail dominance that let a few extreme observations drive the portfolio while leaving the cross-sectional slope flat. Restricting to R&D reporters is economically required here — retrenchment is undefined without a program — and tests whether the previously observed alpha survives in a rank-stable form.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hiring_Binge_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
evaluated.hypothesis: Headcount expansion destroys value when each existing employee already generates little gross profit, because the firm is scaling a labor process with no intangible margin to defend it; at high value-added-per-worker firms new hires embody knowledge capital and are a positive investment.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's `Hiring_Binge_Low_RD_Per_Worker` produced a −3.3% alpha but only a −1.67 FMB t-stat, exactly the signature the critic predicted from every zero-R&D firm tying at the conditioner's extreme; gross profit per employee is a continuous, universally reported measure of the same underlying idea (is labor backed by intangible rents?). This should convert the existing portfolio evidence into cross-sectional evidence without changing the economic channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Acquisition_Wave_Followed_By_Profitability_Trough
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that spent heavily on acquisitions over the past five years and now sit at the bottom of their own five-year gross-profitability range have demonstrably failed to realize the intangible synergies they paid for; the market is slow to mark down the acquired intangible base, so returns are low.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new dynamic channel — cumulative acquisition history validated (or not) by the firm's own profitability history — rather than a contemporaneous acquisition-intensity sort, which should concentrate the short leg on genuine post-merger disappointments instead of on all acquirers. Using a within-firm five-year position rather than a fitted trend keeps the conditioner a bounded state variable, avoiding the sign flips that afflicted the archive's TREND-based conditioners.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt_Raised_Against_Non_Collateral_Intangible_Base
evaluated.hypothesis: Purchased intangibles and goodwill are poor collateral, so debt raised by a firm whose capital base is dominated by intangibles is borrowing against assets that cannot be liquidated at book value; such firms face tighter future financing constraints and forced deleveraging, and subsequently underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the composition-times-gross-profitability family the critic flagged as duplicative and instead tests a financing-frictions channel, deliberately inverting the conditioning of the archive's `Externally_Financed_Tangible_Buildout` (which found a −3.57 FMB slope but zero FF5 alpha when conditioning on *low* intangibles) to ask whether the portfolio-level abnormal return lives in the *high*-intangible corner instead. Using net debt issuance rather than total external finance and scaling the intangible base by book equity keeps both legs continuous and near-universally defined, so no reporting mass point is introduced.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Knowledge_Stock_Explains_Weak_Measured_Profitability
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(xrd, 5), ADD(ppent, ceq))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The gross-profitability premium should not apply to firms whose accumulated R&D is large relative to their recorded capital: their low measured profitability is largely an accounting artifact of expensing knowledge investment during its gestation period, so these firms are misclassified as unprofitable and earn high subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The two legs are now oppositely signed relative to their standalone anomaly directions — high R&D stock predicts high returns but low gross profitability predicts low returns — so the composite cannot be dominated by additive main effects and instead tests whether knowledge intensity switches off the profitability penalty. Dropping COALESCE restricts estimation to firms that actually run research programs, eliminating the zero-R&D tie at the bottom of the rank that the critic identified, at the cost of roughly halved coverage that is intrinsic to the mechanism being tested.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Young_Plant_Vintage_Without_Margin_Support
evaluated.hypothesis: A high net-to-gross PP&E ratio means the physical asset base is young — the firm has recently completed a heavy capital cycle — and when that fresh capacity sits in a business with no gross-margin cushion, the investment was made into a commoditizing market and will not earn its cost of capital.
evaluated.reasoning: Asset vintage is a stock measure of *cumulative recent* investment that is untouched by the archive and is much less collinear with the CMA factor's one-year asset-growth definition, so any alpha is less likely to be spanned by FF5. It is also naturally bounded between zero and one, avoiding the tail concentration that has decoupled FMB slopes from portfolio alphas in the flow-based signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Labor_Bloat_Relative_To_Output_Low_Margin
evaluated.hypothesis: Headcount growing faster than revenue is labor over-investment: the firm is adding fixed human cost without commensurate output, and at low-gross-profit firms there is no intangible margin to absorb the mistake, so returns are low.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's two hiring signals both delivered alphas near −3.5% with FMB t-stats of only −1.7 to −1.8, consistent with raw employment growth being size- and cycle-driven rather than firm-specific over-hiring; differencing against contemporaneous sales growth removes the common cyclical component and should convert portfolio evidence into cross-sectional evidence. The conditioner is unchanged so the comparison isolates the design choice in the investment leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex_Rate_Without_Peer_Relative_Pricing_Power
evaluated.hypothesis: Physical investment is penalized when a firm has no differentiation advantage *relative to its own industry peers*: a below-peer gross margin means the firm holds no brand, technology, or process rent, so adding capacity into a market where competitors are more efficient destroys value.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic's spanning concern is that capex-to-assets times raw gross profitability reproduces CMA×RMW; industry-demeaning the margin removes the industry-level profitability structure that RMW sorts on and turns the conditioner into a firm-specific measure of intangible competitive position, while capex scaled by installed PP&E is an investment *rate* rather than the asset-growth definition CMA uses. Both changes push the construct away from the evaluating factor model while keeping the economics intact.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash_Burned_To_Purchase_Intangible_Assets
evaluated.hypothesis: Converting liquid, verifiable cash into illiquid, unverifiable intangible assets is the sharpest form of managerial empire building: the firm exchanges an asset investors can value at par for one whose worth depends entirely on management's own projections, and such conversions are followed by low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the flow-restatement of the archive's best performer and opens the cash channel, which no evaluated signal has touched, so it cannot be a repackaging of the intangible-composition-times-gross-profitability result. The two legs are sourced from opposite sides of the balance sheet with no mechanical double counting — a firm can add intangibles without depleting cash (equity- or debt-financed) and it is precisely the cash-funded subset the hypothesis targets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Three_Year_Capex_Program_With_No_Revenue_Response
evaluated.hypothesis: A multi-year capital program should show up as incremental revenue; firms that have sustained high cumulative investment while their revenue base is flat or shrinking have built capacity the market does not want, and the write-down of that capacity has not yet been priced.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling both the cumulative capex and the three-year revenue change by total assets removes the exploding 1/capex denominator the critic identified, so the ranking is driven by genuinely heavy-investing, non-growing firms rather than by asset-light noise. Dropping the intangible-composition leg also removes the overlap with the archive conditioner, leaving a cleaner test of investment validated by output over a horizon long enough for capacity to come online — a construct distinct from one-year asset growth.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Stock_Financed_Goodwill_Creation
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm issues equity and simultaneously books large goodwill, it is using its own shares as acquisition currency; managers do this when they believe the stock is overvalued, and the buyer's overvaluation plus the premium paid for unverifiable intangibles compound into low subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than re-running the issuance-times-intangible-intensity cell with the sign flipped, this conditions issuance on *what the proceeds bought* — newly created goodwill — which explains why the archive's tangible-conditioned financing signal had a clean FMB slope but no alpha: undifferentiated external finance mostly funds capex that CMA already spans, whereas stock-financed intangible purchases are a distinct corporate event. Both legs are near-universally defined and no variable is shared between them, so the interaction is not a mechanical identity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity_Overhang_Relative_To_Revenue_Base
evaluated.hypothesis: Physical capacity that has grown faster than the revenue it serves over a three-year horizon is an overhang: the firm has built plant it cannot fill, and at low-margin firms there is no pricing power to absorb the resulting under-utilization.
evaluated.reasoning: `Three_Year_Capex_Program_With_No_Revenue_Response` delivered a −3.3% alpha but a flat +0.20 FMB slope because both legs were asset-scaled dollar quantities with heavy skew; expressing the same economics as a difference of two three-year growth rates is exactly the transformation that converted the hiring-signal family from fmb −1.7 to −2.1 with a better Sharpe. The long horizon also separates this from the one-year investment measures that CMA spans.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capital_Base_At_Peak_Versus_Revenue_Drawdown
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), TS_MAX(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), 5))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, TS_MAX(revt, 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose combined physical and purchased-intangible capital sits at its own five-year maximum while revenue has fallen well below its own five-year peak is carrying an unwritten-down overhang; management has not yet retired capacity or impaired soft assets that the business no longer supports.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the flagship's composition-times-profitability structure entirely and uses a drawdown state — each quantity measured against its own history rather than against the cross-section — which is a different economic object (delayed capacity retirement and delayed impairment) and is not an investment-rate or profitability sort that CMA or RMW can span. Both legs are bounded in [0,1] by construction, which should give a stable cross-sectional ranking rather than the tail-driven spreads that produced flat FMB slopes earlier.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating_Commitments_With_Below_Peer_Margin
evaluated.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), SUB(GROWTH(emp, 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Inventory and headcount are the operating commitments managers add when they expect demand that does not arrive; making both while carrying a below-peer gross margin identifies firms over-extending in a market where competitors are better positioned.
evaluated.reasoning: The weighting objection is resolved by pooling exactly two channels, so each receives one half, and capex is deliberately dropped so the commitment leg contains only working-capital and labor margins that the CMA asset-growth factor does not measure. Industry-demeaning the margin conditioner removes the sector-level profitability structure RMW sorts on, making the surviving variation firm-specific competitive position rather than a repackaged profitability factor.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Goodwill_Heavy_With_Thin_Equity_And_Cash_Buffer
evaluated.hypothesis: Goodwill is the least loss-absorbing asset on the balance sheet, so a firm whose assets are goodwill-heavy while its equity plus cash buffer is thin is one write-down away from technical insolvency; that fragility is not priced until the impairment is announced.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a balance-sheet-fragility channel rather than a capital-productivity one: neither leg contains an investment rate or a profitability measure, so it cannot be a restatement of the flagship or of CMA×RMW, and it asks a question the archive has never posed — how much real capital stands behind the soft assets. Both components are near-universally reported, and combining equity with cash gives a loss-absorption measure that is meaningful even for firms with unusual leverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity_Drain_Without_Margin_Cushion
evaluated.hypothesis: Depleting the cash buffer is sustainable for a high-margin firm reinvesting from strength but is a warning sign at a low-margin firm, where the drain reflects operations consuming liquidity rather than opportunities being funded.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs a specific archive failure: `Cash_Burned_To_Purchase_Intangible_Assets` had a strong cross-sectional slope (fmb −3.66) but zero portfolio alpha because its second leg (intangible purchases scaled by sales) was sparse and lumpy, fragmenting the extreme portfolios. Pairing the same liquidity channel with the conditioner that has repeatedly produced tradable spreads tests whether the cross-sectional signal can be converted into portfolio evidence, while keeping the mechanism (liquidity, not capital composition) distinct from the flagship family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft_Capital_Runoff_With_High_Capital_Turnover
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that let their purchased intangible base run off — amortizing without replacing it through new acquisitions — while turning their remaining capital rapidly into revenue are running an efficient, self-funding operation whose lack of headline growth causes it to be overlooked.
evaluated.reasoning: The prior long-side attempt was a low-investment, high-gross-profitability position that CMA and RMW mechanically absorb; this version replaces physical disinvestment with *intangible* balance-sheet run-off and replaces margin with capital turnover, neither of which is an FF5 factor construction. It targets the archive's persistent weakness — every reliable result so far is short-side driven with modest Sharpe — by testing whether an economically distinct long state carries abnormal return.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft_Capital_Runoff_With_Cash_Accumulation
evaluated.hypothesis: Genuine harvesting shows up as soft capital running off the balance sheet while cash builds: the firm is converting acquired intangibles into realized cash rather than replacing them with new purchases, and this self-funding discipline is underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This extends the archive's best Sharpe result by replacing its capital-turnover conditioner with the mirror image of the validated liquidity channel, so the two legs now describe the same managerial decision from the asset and the cash side — a stronger economic claim than run-off plus a static efficiency ratio. It also tests whether the liquidity axis is symmetric: the drain predicts poorly on the short side, so accumulation paired with soft-capital discipline should predict well on the long side.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Investing_Through_A_Revenue_Drawdown
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm still running a high physical investment rate while its revenue sits far below its own five-year peak is investing in denial: management is committing capital to capacity the market has already told it is unwanted.
evaluated.reasoning: `Capital_Base_At_Peak_Versus_Revenue_Drawdown` proved the revenue-drawdown conditioner is powerful cross-sectionally (fmb −4.47) but produced no alpha because both of its legs were slow-moving, near-permanent states that FF5 spans; pairing the same bounded conditioner with a fast-moving annual investment rate should give the portfolio the turnover it needs to escape the factor model. The construct also differs from the archive's margin-conditioned capex signals by conditioning on demand realization rather than profitability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Erratic_Capital_Policy_With_Soft_Asset_Base
evaluated.hypothesis: Unstable investment policy — a capital expenditure rate that swings widely from year to year — signals weak capital-allocation discipline, and this is most damaging at firms whose assets are already dominated by unverifiable purchased intangibles, where outside monitoring is hardest.
evaluated.reasoning: Second-moment investment behavior is an entirely unexplored construct in this archive and is orthogonal by construction to the level and growth measures that CMA spans, so any alpha cannot be a repackaged investment factor. The interaction is genuinely conditional: policy instability is tolerable when assets are hard and verifiable, but it is a governance red flag when the balance sheet cannot be independently valued.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Working_Capital_Discipline_With_High_Capital_Turnover
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms shrinking inventory relative to their own sales growth while already generating high revenue per dollar of total capital are tightening an efficient operation; the absence of headline growth causes the market to overlook the improving cash conversion.
evaluated.reasoning: The long side has now been shown to work through capital turnover, but only via the intangible run-off margin; testing the working-capital margin under the same conditioner establishes whether the positive-side effect is a general capital-discipline phenomenon or specific to soft-asset amortization. The growth-differential form is the construction that repaired the FMB slope in the labor family, so it should deliver cross-sectional as well as portfolio evidence.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity_Drain_At_Soft_Asset_Firms
evaluated.hypothesis: A shrinking cash buffer is far more dangerous when the remaining assets are purchased intangibles rather than plant, because soft assets cannot be pledged or sold quickly; the firm that burns cash while holding unpledgeable capital is the one that will have to raise equity from weakness or impair.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than blending two evaluated signals under their shared gross-margin conditioner, this tests the previously unexamined cell where the two validated axes meet each other directly — liquidity flow conditioned on asset softness, with no profitability leg at all — so the result speaks to whether the axes interact or merely add. Scaling intangibles by sales rather than by a capital base gives a soft-capital-intensity measure distinct from the composition ratio used elsewhere in the archive, and both legs are near-universally reported.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Stale_Goodwill_Overdue_For_Impairment
evaluated.hypothesis: Goodwill that is large relative to recent acquisition spending is legacy goodwill carried at cost from older deals; when the firm's revenue has also fallen well below its own five-year peak, the economic case for that carrying value has lapsed and a write-down is overdue but not yet priced.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a conditioner swap with a new economic object — the vintage of unimpaired goodwill, measured as the stock relative to the flow that would have created it — which no archive signal has constructed and which is not an investment rate or a profitability sort. It pairs that stock with the bounded revenue-drawdown state that produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope, while avoiding that signal's fatal flaw (two slow-moving persistent legs) because goodwill staleness changes discretely when deals or write-offs occur.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft_Investment_Drift_Versus_Installed_Mix
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)), ADD(capx, ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)))), RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When the marginal investment dollar is far softer than the installed asset base, the firm is drifting away from the business it knows — buying intangibles and companies rather than reinvesting in its own operations — and that drift destroys value most at firms whose existing capital already generates little revenue.
evaluated.reasoning: The construct compares the *composition of the flow* to the *composition of the stock*, a within-firm benchmark that no archive signal has used and that is scale-free and centered at zero by design, so it measures strategic drift rather than the level of investment or intangibility. Pairing it with the capital-turnover conditioner that has powered the archive's best results on both sides tests whether drift is punished specifically where the core business is already unproductive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Short_Maturity_Debt_Against_Goodwill_Heavy_Equity
evaluated.hypothesis: Funding a goodwill-dominated equity base with debt that must be rolled over within the year creates refinancing risk against assets that cannot secure new lending; when credit conditions tighten these firms are forced to impair, dilute, or fire-sale.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive tested debt *issuance* against intangible intensity (weak on both metrics), but never the maturity structure of existing debt, which is the dimension that actually determines rollover exposure and is not an investment-rate or profitability sort that FF5 can span. Both legs are stock ratios reported by essentially all firms, so coverage should sit near the archive maximum and the portfolio composition should be stable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity_Added_Without_Staffing_Low_Margin
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(MIN(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), SUB(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), GROWTH(emp, 1)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))

evaluated.name: Thin_Cash_Coverage_Of_Operating_Costs_With_Soft_Assets
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for a soft-asset firm is not the direction of its cash balance but how many months of operating cost that balance covers: a firm with thin cash relative to its cost base and no pledgeable assets has no way to fund a bad year except dilution or asset write-offs.

The interaction is then genuinely conditional: runway is only binding when the remaining assets cannot be pledged, which is precisely what the intangible share measures.

evaluated.name: Soft_Capital_Being_Validated_In_Real_Time
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(revt, 1), GROWTH(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), 1))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The flagship result says soft capital that fails to produce output is overpriced; the symmetric and untested claim is that soft capital which is *demonstrably* producing more output per year — revenue growing faster than the capital base — is underpriced, because investors discount intangible-heavy balance sheets indiscriminately.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the mechanical merger of two evaluated long-side signals with a new economic claim: it is the *improvement* in capital productivity, not its level, that identifies which intangible-heavy firms deserve their carrying values, and the conditioning direction (high soft-asset share) is the opposite of every prior negative signal, so the result is not predictable from the parents. Both legs are near-universally reported and the growth differential is scale-free, giving stable cross-sectional ranking.

evaluated.name: Roll_Up_Failing_To_Lift_Labor_Productivity
evaluated.hypothesis: The standard justification for a serial acquisition program is that combining organizations raises output per employee; a three-year acquisition wave followed by flat or falling revenue per worker is direct evidence that the promised synergies never arrived.
evaluated.reasoning: Measuring labor productivity as a three-year *within-firm growth rate* rather than a level removes the industry determination the critic flagged, since each firm is benchmarked against its own pre-acquisition productivity rather than against firms with different vertical integration. Matching the horizon of the productivity test to the horizon of the acquisition program makes this an integration-failure test rather than a conditioner swap on the flagship, and it differs from the archive's acquisition-wave signal by using output per worker instead of a profitability position.

evaluated.name: Soft_Investment_In_Place_Of_Hard_Investment
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)), capx), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent)))))

evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))

If the cash-adjusted version strengthens the result it identifies the conversion channel; if it does not, the flagship is a pure margin effect and the final generation should stop refining it.

evaluated.name: Cash_Position_At_Own_Five_Year_Low_With_Soft_Assets
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose cash relative to its own sales base sits at the bottom of its five-year range has exhausted the buffer it normally operates with; when its remaining assets are unpledgeable intangibles, that depletion cannot be reversed by borrowing against collateral.

evaluated.name: Short_Term_Debt_Load_With_Goodwill_Heavy_Revenue_Base
evaluated.hypothesis: Carrying a large stock of debt due within the year is a genuine refinancing burden only in proportion to firm size, and it becomes dangerous when a large part of the asset base is goodwill rather than revenue-producing collateral, because lenders reprice or withdraw and the equity absorbs the adjustment.
evaluated.reasoning: Scale is retained by keeping the archive's original `dlc/at` leg untouched, so this makes exactly one change to `Short_Maturity_Debt_Against_Goodwill_Heavy_Equity`: replacing the `gdwl/ceq` conditioner, whose near-zero and negative denominators inverted the ranking for the most fragile firms, with goodwill per dollar of revenue, which is monotone and always well defined. That isolation makes the −4.7% alpha with a +0.23 slope interpretable — if the slope turns negative, the denominator pathology was the cause.

evaluated.name: Fully_Depreciated_Plant_Still_Earning_Rents
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ppent, ppegt))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))))

evaluated.name: Acquiring_When_Own_Labor_Productivity_Is_Depressed
evaluated.hypothesis: Managers buy revenue when their own organization has stopped producing it: purchasing companies and intangibles while output per employee sits at the bottom of its five-year range is a defensive deal made from operational weakness, and such deals disappoint.

Benchmarking labor productivity within the firm's own history also removes the industry determination that makes raw sales-per-employee unusable, and the timing framing (state *before* the deal) distinguishes this from the archive's post-acquisition disappointment signals.

evaluated.name: Net_Short_Term_Funding_Gap_With_Goodwill_Heavy_Revenue
evaluated.hypothesis: What determines refinancing exposure is the shortfall between debt coming due and cash on hand; when that gap is positive and the asset base backing it is goodwill rather than revenue-producing collateral, the firm must refinance on worse terms and the equity bears the repricing.

evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))

evaluated.name: Old_Plant_And_No_Purchased_Intangibles
evaluated.hypothesis: The archetypal underpriced firm on this axis operates written-down physical capacity and buys no soft capital: its assets are real, proven, and carried below economic value, and management is not spending shareholder money on unverifiable purchases.

evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A positive net short-term funding gap is survivable for a firm generating cash profit and dangerous for one that is not; the interaction of refinancing need with cash-generation failure identifies firms that must refinance precisely when they cannot self-fund.

If the slope remains flat with a large alpha, the conclusion is that this channel is genuinely factor-hedged rather than mismeasured.

evaluated.name: Debt_Financed_Goodwill_Creation
evaluated.hypothesis: Goodwill created by a highly levered acquirer is the most fragile asset on any balance sheet: the premium was funded with fixed claims that must be serviced from the target's cash flows, so any shortfall forces impairment and equity value transfers to creditors.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive tested stock-financed goodwill creation and found the *opposite* sign (alpha +3.3%), which is consistent with equity-funded deals being cushioned by flexible claims; the debt-funded cell is the untested complement and the mechanism predicts the reverse. Both legs are near-universally defined, the leverage ratio is bounded between zero and one so it avoids the negative-equity pathology that broke earlier goodwill-to-equity constructs, and no variable is shared between the two legs.

evaluated.name: Soft_Asset_Base_With_Starved_Physical_Reinvestment
evaluated.hypothesis: Low physical reinvestment means opposite things depending on what the firm owns: for a hard-asset firm with rents it is harvesting written-down capacity, but for a firm whose balance sheet is dominated by purchased intangibles it means the entire asset base is decaying — soft capital that cannot be verified and hard capital that is not being maintained.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a genuinely new cell rather than a deflator change: the archive established that written-down plant earning rents is *underpriced* (fmb +5.04) and that soft capital is overpriced, and the natural test of whether both findings share one asset-quality mechanism is to combine low reinvestment with a soft rather than hard asset base, where the prediction reverses. The two legs share no variable, both are near-universally reported, and the reinvestment rate scaled by gross plant is a maintenance measure not previously paired with intangible intensity.

evaluated.name: Soft_Capital_With_Cost_Ratio_At_Own_Five_Year_High
evaluated.hypothesis: The soft-capital effect should be concentrated not in firms with structurally low margins but in firms whose own cost-to-sales ratio has just climbed to the top of its five-year range: that deterioration is the operational evidence that the acquired intangibles are losing their economic value and an impairment is approaching.
evaluated.reasoning: Every conditioner that has worked in this archive measures a cross-sectional *level* of profitability, which confounds business-model differences with deterioration; benchmarking the cost ratio against the firm's own five-year history isolates deterioration and asks a question the drift construct cannot — whether it is the turning point, not the level, that identifies mispriced soft capital. The bounded within-firm state avoids the persistence that neutralized the earlier peak-versus-drawdown design, and the conditioner is a cost-side measure never used in the archive.

considered.name: Goodwill_Fueled_Expansion
considered.hypothesis: Balance-sheet expansion that is financed by acquired goodwill rather than internally generated capital reflects empire building and overpayment for purchased intangibles, and should be followed by low abnormal returns.
considered.reasoning: The asset-growth anomaly is strongest when the growth is inorganic, because goodwill additions capitalize the premium paid in acquisitions and are prone to later impairment. Multiplying the rank of total asset growth by the rank of goodwill-driven growth isolates firms whose expansion is simultaneously large and acquisition-intangible in nature, an interaction neither theme captures alone.

considered.name: Externally_Financed_Tangible_Buildout
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 1), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(xrd, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Raising external debt and equity to fund expansion is most value-destructive at intangible-poor firms, which lack the knowledge assets needed to earn a spread over the cost of the new capital.
considered.reasoning: The external-financing anomaly and the intangible-intensity premium point in opposite directions, so their interaction should sharpen both: capital raised by intangible-lean, commodity-like producers is the clearest case of overinvestment. Conditioning the financing measure on low intangible intensity makes the mechanism about who is raising the money, not merely how much.

considered.name: Growth_With_Weak_Intangible_Productivity
considered.hypothesis: Asset growth predicts low returns mainly when the existing capital base, measured inclusive of recognized intangibles, is already generating little revenue per dollar deployed; growth by capital-efficient firms is a positive-NPV signal instead.
considered.reasoning: Sales per unit of combined tangible and intangible capital is a direct measure of whether prior investment has been converted into output, so it identifies which growers are compounding an unproductive asset base. The interaction conditions the classic investment effect on intangible-inclusive capital productivity rather than treating all growth identically.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Knowledge_Pivot_Capex_Retrenchment
considered.hypothesis: A cut in the physical investment rate carries very different information depending on where the firm's productive capacity resides: for R&D-intensive firms it signals a deliberate pivot toward knowledge production (asset-light, high expected returns on expensed intangible capital), whereas for tangible-capital firms it is closer to ordinary capacity contraction.
considered.reasoning: The expression is multiplicative rather than additive, so it only lights up when a high R&D-to-assets firm simultaneously reduces its capex-to-PP&E rate, which is exactly the conditional claim rather than a sum of the R&D premium and the investment-decline effect. Scaling capex by the installed PP&E base and taking its first difference removes the mechanical "ratio rises because capex fell" artifact of the earlier mix variable, and using reported xrd (no zero-fill) prevents a large point mass at zero from destroying cross-sectional discrimination, at the cost of restricting the sample to firms for which the knowledge-pivot mechanism is even defined.

considered.name: Plant_Buildout_Without_Knowledge_Capital
considered.hypothesis: The return penalty on gross plant expansion is concentrated among firms with essentially no accumulated knowledge capital, because capacity added without proprietary technology competes away its own rents; the same expansion by research-rich firms complements existing intangible capital and is not penalized.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the rank difference with a rank product makes the signal extreme only in the joint corner (fast PP&E growth AND a thin five-year R&D stock), which is the interaction the hypothesis asserts and which cannot be produced by stacking the PP&E-growth and R&D-intensity anomalies. Cumulating R&D over five years and scaling by sales measures the depth of the knowledge moat rather than one year of spending, and zero-filling is economically appropriate here because genuinely non-innovating firms are the intended conditioning group.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Acquisitions_By_Non_Innovators
considered.hypothesis: Acquisition-driven growth destroys value mainly when the acquirer has no internal research capability: such firms buy growth options at a competitive control premium precisely because they cannot build them, and they lack the absorptive capacity to integrate acquired technology.
considered.reasoning: The multiplicative form tests whether acquirer underperformance is state-dependent on the buyer's own knowledge stock, rather than blending two standalone anomalies with a rank difference; a research-intensive serial acquirer and a research-barren one receive very different scores at identical acquisition intensity. It is also mechanically distinct from the accepted goodwill signal, which keys on total asset growth financed by goodwill additions rather than on cash acquisition intensity conditioned on absent internal R&D.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Acquired_Growth_Without_Organic_Revenue
considered.hypothesis: Buying growth is value-destructive precisely when the firm's own top line is stalling: managers of decelerating businesses overpay for targets, and the purchase premium booked as goodwill is later impaired.
considered.reasoning: Gen-0's acquisition signal delivered a big alpha but a −0.8 FMB t-stat because its conditioner (five-year R&D/sales) is essentially an industry dummy with a mass point at zero; replacing it with firm-level organic revenue growth gives a continuous, firm-specific measure of *why* the firm is acquiring. Combining cash acquisition spend with the contemporaneous goodwill addition captures both the outlay and the unidentifiable-intangible premium in a single scaled flow.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Hiring_Binge_Low_RD_Per_Worker
considered.hypothesis: Rapid headcount expansion is a negative-return investment signal when each worker is backed by little research spending, because such labor is a low-skill fixed cost added at the cycle peak; at knowledge-intensive firms new hires embody intangible capital formation.
considered.reasoning: This opens a distinct economic channel — labor as an investment margin — and R&D per employee is a firm-specific knowledge-intensity measure that is far less collinear with industry membership than R&D/sales. Employment growth is also nearly orthogonal to the CMA construction, so any alpha here is less likely to be absorbed by FF5.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex_Commitment_With_Bloating_Knowledge_Capital
considered.hypothesis: When a firm's stock of knowledge and recognized intangible capital keeps growing relative to the revenue it generates, the intangible base is failing to convert into sales; continuing to commit physical capital on top of that unproductive intangible base is overinvestment and is followed by low returns.
considered.reasoning: The mechanical coupling the critic flagged is removed because the investment leg (capx over installed PP&E) shares no variable with the conditioner, whose denominator is revenue rather than a capital base that capex inflates. It also changes the economic object from a static productivity level (the archive signal) to a multi-year deterioration in the revenue yield of intangible capital, and dividing by revt rather than by a possibly-zero intangible stock keeps the ratio well defined for the broad sample.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex_Push_Amid_Research_Retrenchment
considered.hypothesis: A firm that is simultaneously ramping physical spending and cutting its smoothed research budget is harvesting a maturing franchise: the visible capex is read as growth by investors while the quiet research cut reveals that the underlying product pipeline is being wound down.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are now firm-level flow growth rates with no sales scaling, eliminating the "ratio moves because the denominator moved" artifact in the previous conditioner. Dropping COALESCE removes the degenerate mass of exactly-zero deltas at non-reporting firms, so the interaction is estimated only where a research-retrenchment decision actually exists, and smoothing R&D over three years ensures the cut reflects strategy rather than a one-year timing blip.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity_Expansion_Into_Eroding_Rents
considered.hypothesis: Gross margin is the realized cash return on a firm's intangible assets — brand, technology, and customer franchise — so a multi-year margin slide means those rents are eroding; firms that expand physical capacity into an eroding franchise are adding capacity to a commoditizing business and earn low subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the industry-neutralization robustness exercise with a different economic channel: the conditioner is the *realized output* of intangible capital rather than another measure of intangible input spending, so it is not a restatement of the archive's R&D-intensity leg. Because sale and cogs are near-universally reported, the conditioner has no zero mass point and full coverage, and its trend form captures franchise decay rather than a single noisy year.

considered.name: Acquired_Intangible_Heavy_Base_Low_Gross_Profitability
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0)), ADD(ppent, ADD(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A capital base dominated by purchased intangibles and goodwill rather than productive plant is only justified if those intangibles generate gross profit; when gross profitability is low, the carrying value is impairment-prone and the firm's past acquisition-driven investment was value-destroying, predicting low returns.
considered.reasoning: The previous share collapsed to 1.0 for every non-R&D reporter, but this composition measure uses balance-sheet stocks whose denominator always contains PP&E, so it is continuous and defined across the whole sample rather than acting as a reporting dummy. The mechanism is also different from the archive's financing and acquisition-flow signals: it asks whether the *accumulated* mix of purchased intangible versus physical capital is being validated by gross profit, making impairment risk, not current investment intensity, the source of predictability.

considered.name: Inventory_Buildup_Without_Pricing_Power
considered.hypothesis: Inventory accumulation is an investment decision whose payoff depends on brand and product differentiation: a commodity producer with no gross-margin cushion that builds stock is producing goods it will have to discount, whereas a high-margin, brand-supported firm can carry inventory profitably.
considered.reasoning: This opens the working-capital investment margin, which is untouched by the archive and largely orthogonal to CMA's asset-growth construction, while retaining the level gross-margin conditioner that has been the archive's most reliable intangible leg. Coverage is essentially full because inventory, sales, and cost of goods are near-universally reported, avoiding the zero-mass problem that has broken the FMB slopes of the R&D-conditioned signals.
