considered.name: Physical_Investment_With_RD_At_Own_History_Low
considered.hypothesis: Among firms that actually run research programs, pushing physical capital while research spending sits at the bottom of its own five-year range signals a deliberate wind-down of the innovation pipeline in favor of harvesting existing capacity, and such firms subsequently underperform.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the diagnosis of `Capex_Push_Amid_Research_Retrenchment`, whose −5.1% alpha coexisted with a null FMB slope: replacing an unbounded growth rate with a bounded position-in-own-history statistic removes the tail dominance that let a few extreme observations drive the portfolio while leaving the cross-sectional slope flat. Restricting to R&D reporters is economically required here — retrenchment is undefined without a program — and tests whether the previously observed alpha survives in a rank-stable form.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Hiring_Binge_Low_Value_Added_Per_Worker
considered.hypothesis: Headcount expansion destroys value when each existing employee already generates little gross profit, because the firm is scaling a labor process with no intangible margin to defend it; at high value-added-per-worker firms new hires embody knowledge capital and are a positive investment.
considered.reasoning: The archive's `Hiring_Binge_Low_RD_Per_Worker` produced a −3.3% alpha but only a −1.67 FMB t-stat, exactly the signature the critic predicted from every zero-R&D firm tying at the conditioner's extreme; gross profit per employee is a continuous, universally reported measure of the same underlying idea (is labor backed by intangible rents?). This should convert the existing portfolio evidence into cross-sectional evidence without changing the economic channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Acquisition_Wave_Followed_By_Profitability_Trough
considered.hypothesis: Firms that spent heavily on acquisitions over the past five years and now sit at the bottom of their own five-year gross-profitability range have demonstrably failed to realize the intangible synergies they paid for; the market is slow to mark down the acquired intangible base, so returns are low.
considered.reasoning: This is a new dynamic channel — cumulative acquisition history validated (or not) by the firm's own profitability history — rather than a contemporaneous acquisition-intensity sort, which should concentrate the short leg on genuine post-merger disappointments instead of on all acquirers. Using a within-firm five-year position rather than a fitted trend keeps the conditioner a bounded state variable, avoiding the sign flips that afflicted the archive's TREND-based conditioners.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt_Raised_Against_Non_Collateral_Intangible_Base
considered.hypothesis: Purchased intangibles and goodwill are poor collateral, so debt raised by a firm whose capital base is dominated by intangibles is borrowing against assets that cannot be liquidated at book value; such firms face tighter future financing constraints and forced deleveraging, and subsequently underperform.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the composition-times-gross-profitability family the critic flagged as duplicative and instead tests a financing-frictions channel, deliberately inverting the conditioning of the archive's `Externally_Financed_Tangible_Buildout` (which found a −3.57 FMB slope but zero FF5 alpha when conditioning on *low* intangibles) to ask whether the portfolio-level abnormal return lives in the *high*-intangible corner instead. Using net debt issuance rather than total external finance and scaling the intangible base by book equity keeps both legs continuous and near-universally defined, so no reporting mass point is introduced.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Knowledge_Stock_Explains_Weak_Measured_Profitability
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(xrd, 5), ADD(ppent, ceq))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))
considered.hypothesis: The gross-profitability premium should not apply to firms whose accumulated R&D is large relative to their recorded capital: their low measured profitability is largely an accounting artifact of expensing knowledge investment during its gestation period, so these firms are misclassified as unprofitable and earn high subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: The two legs are now oppositely signed relative to their standalone anomaly directions — high R&D stock predicts high returns but low gross profitability predicts low returns — so the composite cannot be dominated by additive main effects and instead tests whether knowledge intensity switches off the profitability penalty. Dropping COALESCE restricts estimation to firms that actually run research programs, eliminating the zero-R&D tie at the bottom of the rank that the critic identified, at the cost of roughly halved coverage that is intrinsic to the mechanism being tested.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Young_Plant_Vintage_Without_Margin_Support
considered.hypothesis: A high net-to-gross PP&E ratio means the physical asset base is young — the firm has recently completed a heavy capital cycle — and when that fresh capacity sits in a business with no gross-margin cushion, the investment was made into a commoditizing market and will not earn its cost of capital.
considered.reasoning: Asset vintage is a stock measure of *cumulative recent* investment that is untouched by the archive and is much less collinear with the CMA factor's one-year asset-growth definition, so any alpha is less likely to be spanned by FF5. It is also naturally bounded between zero and one, avoiding the tail concentration that has decoupled FMB slopes from portfolio alphas in the flow-based signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Labor_Bloat_Relative_To_Output_Low_Margin
considered.hypothesis: Headcount growing faster than revenue is labor over-investment: the firm is adding fixed human cost without commensurate output, and at low-gross-profit firms there is no intangible margin to absorb the mistake, so returns are low.
considered.reasoning: The archive's two hiring signals both delivered alphas near −3.5% with FMB t-stats of only −1.7 to −1.8, consistent with raw employment growth being size- and cycle-driven rather than firm-specific over-hiring; differencing against contemporaneous sales growth removes the common cyclical component and should convert portfolio evidence into cross-sectional evidence. The conditioner is unchanged so the comparison isolates the design choice in the investment leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex_Rate_Without_Peer_Relative_Pricing_Power
considered.hypothesis: Physical investment is penalized when a firm has no differentiation advantage *relative to its own industry peers*: a below-peer gross margin means the firm holds no brand, technology, or process rent, so adding capacity into a market where competitors are more efficient destroys value.
considered.reasoning: The critic's spanning concern is that capex-to-assets times raw gross profitability reproduces CMA×RMW; industry-demeaning the margin removes the industry-level profitability structure that RMW sorts on and turns the conditioner into a firm-specific measure of intangible competitive position, while capex scaled by installed PP&E is an investment *rate* rather than the asset-growth definition CMA uses. Both changes push the construct away from the evaluating factor model while keeping the economics intact.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash_Burned_To_Purchase_Intangible_Assets
considered.hypothesis: Converting liquid, verifiable cash into illiquid, unverifiable intangible assets is the sharpest form of managerial empire building: the firm exchanges an asset investors can value at par for one whose worth depends entirely on management's own projections, and such conversions are followed by low returns.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the flow-restatement of the archive's best performer and opens the cash channel, which no evaluated signal has touched, so it cannot be a repackaging of the intangible-composition-times-gross-profitability result. The two legs are sourced from opposite sides of the balance sheet with no mechanical double counting — a firm can add intangibles without depleting cash (equity- or debt-financed) and it is precisely the cash-funded subset the hypothesis targets.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Three_Year_Capex_Program_With_No_Revenue_Response
considered.hypothesis: A multi-year capital program should show up as incremental revenue; firms that have sustained high cumulative investment while their revenue base is flat or shrinking have built capacity the market does not want, and the write-down of that capacity has not yet been priced.
considered.reasoning: Scaling both the cumulative capex and the three-year revenue change by total assets removes the exploding 1/capex denominator the critic identified, so the ranking is driven by genuinely heavy-investing, non-growing firms rather than by asset-light noise. Dropping the intangible-composition leg also removes the overlap with the archive conditioner, leaving a cleaner test of investment validated by output over a horizon long enough for capacity to come online — a construct distinct from one-year asset growth.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Stock_Financed_Goodwill_Creation
considered.hypothesis: When a firm issues equity and simultaneously books large goodwill, it is using its own shares as acquisition currency; managers do this when they believe the stock is overvalued, and the buyer's overvaluation plus the premium paid for unverifiable intangibles compound into low subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Rather than re-running the issuance-times-intangible-intensity cell with the sign flipped, this conditions issuance on *what the proceeds bought* — newly created goodwill — which explains why the archive's tangible-conditioned financing signal had a clean FMB slope but no alpha: undifferentiated external finance mostly funds capex that CMA already spans, whereas stock-financed intangible purchases are a distinct corporate event. Both legs are near-universally defined and no variable is shared between them, so the interaction is not a mechanical identity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity_Overhang_Relative_To_Revenue_Base
considered.hypothesis: Physical capacity that has grown faster than the revenue it serves over a three-year horizon is an overhang: the firm has built plant it cannot fill, and at low-margin firms there is no pricing power to absorb the resulting under-utilization.
considered.reasoning: `Three_Year_Capex_Program_With_No_Revenue_Response` delivered a −3.3% alpha but a flat +0.20 FMB slope because both legs were asset-scaled dollar quantities with heavy skew; expressing the same economics as a difference of two three-year growth rates is exactly the transformation that converted the hiring-signal family from fmb −1.7 to −2.1 with a better Sharpe. The long horizon also separates this from the one-year investment measures that CMA spans.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capital_Base_At_Peak_Versus_Revenue_Drawdown
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), TS_MAX(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), 5))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, TS_MAX(revt, 5)))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose combined physical and purchased-intangible capital sits at its own five-year maximum while revenue has fallen well below its own five-year peak is carrying an unwritten-down overhang; management has not yet retired capacity or impaired soft assets that the business no longer supports.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the flagship's composition-times-profitability structure entirely and uses a drawdown state — each quantity measured against its own history rather than against the cross-section — which is a different economic object (delayed capacity retirement and delayed impairment) and is not an investment-rate or profitability sort that CMA or RMW can span. Both legs are bounded in [0,1] by construction, which should give a stable cross-sectional ranking rather than the tail-driven spreads that produced flat FMB slopes earlier.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Operating_Commitments_With_Below_Peer_Margin
considered.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), SUB(GROWTH(emp, 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
considered.hypothesis: Inventory and headcount are the operating commitments managers add when they expect demand that does not arrive; making both while carrying a below-peer gross margin identifies firms over-extending in a market where competitors are better positioned.
considered.reasoning: The weighting objection is resolved by pooling exactly two channels, so each receives one half, and capex is deliberately dropped so the commitment leg contains only working-capital and labor margins that the CMA asset-growth factor does not measure. Industry-demeaning the margin conditioner removes the sector-level profitability structure RMW sorts on, making the surviving variation firm-specific competitive position rather than a repackaged profitability factor.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill_Heavy_With_Thin_Equity_And_Cash_Buffer
considered.hypothesis: Goodwill is the least loss-absorbing asset on the balance sheet, so a firm whose assets are goodwill-heavy while its equity plus cash buffer is thin is one write-down away from technical insolvency; that fragility is not priced until the impairment is announced.
considered.reasoning: This is a balance-sheet-fragility channel rather than a capital-productivity one: neither leg contains an investment rate or a profitability measure, so it cannot be a restatement of the flagship or of CMA×RMW, and it asks a question the archive has never posed — how much real capital stands behind the soft assets. Both components are near-universally reported, and combining equity with cash gives a loss-absorption measure that is meaningful even for firms with unusual leverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Liquidity_Drain_Without_Margin_Cushion
considered.hypothesis: Depleting the cash buffer is sustainable for a high-margin firm reinvesting from strength but is a warning sign at a low-margin firm, where the drain reflects operations consuming liquidity rather than opportunities being funded.
considered.reasoning: This repairs a specific archive failure: `Cash_Burned_To_Purchase_Intangible_Assets` had a strong cross-sectional slope (fmb −3.66) but zero portfolio alpha because its second leg (intangible purchases scaled by sales) was sparse and lumpy, fragmenting the extreme portfolios. Pairing the same liquidity channel with the conditioner that has repeatedly produced tradable spreads tests whether the cross-sectional signal can be converted into portfolio evidence, while keeping the mechanism (liquidity, not capital composition) distinct from the flagship family.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Capital_Runoff_With_High_Capital_Turnover
considered.hypothesis: Firms that let their purchased intangible base run off — amortizing without replacing it through new acquisitions — while turning their remaining capital rapidly into revenue are running an efficient, self-funding operation whose lack of headline growth causes it to be overlooked.
considered.reasoning: The prior long-side attempt was a low-investment, high-gross-profitability position that CMA and RMW mechanically absorb; this version replaces physical disinvestment with *intangible* balance-sheet run-off and replaces margin with capital turnover, neither of which is an FF5 factor construction. It targets the archive's persistent weakness — every reliable result so far is short-side driven with modest Sharpe — by testing whether an economically distinct long state carries abnormal return.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Capital_Runoff_With_Cash_Accumulation
considered.hypothesis: Genuine harvesting shows up as soft capital running off the balance sheet while cash builds: the firm is converting acquired intangibles into realized cash rather than replacing them with new purchases, and this self-funding discipline is underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This extends the archive's best Sharpe result by replacing its capital-turnover conditioner with the mirror image of the validated liquidity channel, so the two legs now describe the same managerial decision from the asset and the cash side — a stronger economic claim than run-off plus a static efficiency ratio. It also tests whether the liquidity axis is symmetric: the drain predicts poorly on the short side, so accumulation paired with soft-capital discipline should predict well on the long side.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Investing_Through_A_Revenue_Drawdown
considered.hypothesis: A firm still running a high physical investment rate while its revenue sits far below its own five-year peak is investing in denial: management is committing capital to capacity the market has already told it is unwanted.
considered.reasoning: `Capital_Base_At_Peak_Versus_Revenue_Drawdown` proved the revenue-drawdown conditioner is powerful cross-sectionally (fmb −4.47) but produced no alpha because both of its legs were slow-moving, near-permanent states that FF5 spans; pairing the same bounded conditioner with a fast-moving annual investment rate should give the portfolio the turnover it needs to escape the factor model. The construct also differs from the archive's margin-conditioned capex signals by conditioning on demand realization rather than profitability.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Erratic_Capital_Policy_With_Soft_Asset_Base
considered.hypothesis: Unstable investment policy — a capital expenditure rate that swings widely from year to year — signals weak capital-allocation discipline, and this is most damaging at firms whose assets are already dominated by unverifiable purchased intangibles, where outside monitoring is hardest.
considered.reasoning: Second-moment investment behavior is an entirely unexplored construct in this archive and is orthogonal by construction to the level and growth measures that CMA spans, so any alpha cannot be a repackaged investment factor. The interaction is genuinely conditional: policy instability is tolerable when assets are hard and verifiable, but it is a governance red flag when the balance sheet cannot be independently valued.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Working_Capital_Discipline_With_High_Capital_Turnover
considered.hypothesis: Firms shrinking inventory relative to their own sales growth while already generating high revenue per dollar of total capital are tightening an efficient operation; the absence of headline growth causes the market to overlook the improving cash conversion.
considered.reasoning: The long side has now been shown to work through capital turnover, but only via the intangible run-off margin; testing the working-capital margin under the same conditioner establishes whether the positive-side effect is a general capital-discipline phenomenon or specific to soft-asset amortization. The growth-differential form is the construction that repaired the FMB slope in the labor family, so it should deliver cross-sectional as well as portfolio evidence.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Liquidity_Drain_At_Soft_Asset_Firms
considered.hypothesis: A shrinking cash buffer is far more dangerous when the remaining assets are purchased intangibles rather than plant, because soft assets cannot be pledged or sold quickly; the firm that burns cash while holding unpledgeable capital is the one that will have to raise equity from weakness or impair.
considered.reasoning: Rather than blending two evaluated signals under their shared gross-margin conditioner, this tests the previously unexamined cell where the two validated axes meet each other directly — liquidity flow conditioned on asset softness, with no profitability leg at all — so the result speaks to whether the axes interact or merely add. Scaling intangibles by sales rather than by a capital base gives a soft-capital-intensity measure distinct from the composition ratio used elsewhere in the archive, and both legs are near-universally reported.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Stale_Goodwill_Overdue_For_Impairment
considered.hypothesis: Goodwill that is large relative to recent acquisition spending is legacy goodwill carried at cost from older deals; when the firm's revenue has also fallen well below its own five-year peak, the economic case for that carrying value has lapsed and a write-down is overdue but not yet priced.
considered.reasoning: This replaces a conditioner swap with a new economic object — the vintage of unimpaired goodwill, measured as the stock relative to the flow that would have created it — which no archive signal has constructed and which is not an investment rate or a profitability sort. It pairs that stock with the bounded revenue-drawdown state that produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope, while avoiding that signal's fatal flaw (two slow-moving persistent legs) because goodwill staleness changes discretely when deals or write-offs occur.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Investment_Drift_Versus_Installed_Mix
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)), ADD(capx, ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)))), RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent)))))
considered.hypothesis: When the marginal investment dollar is far softer than the installed asset base, the firm is drifting away from the business it knows — buying intangibles and companies rather than reinvesting in its own operations — and that drift destroys value most at firms whose existing capital already generates little revenue.
considered.reasoning: The construct compares the *composition of the flow* to the *composition of the stock*, a within-firm benchmark that no archive signal has used and that is scale-free and centered at zero by design, so it measures strategic drift rather than the level of investment or intangibility. Pairing it with the capital-turnover conditioner that has powered the archive's best results on both sides tests whether drift is punished specifically where the core business is already unproductive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Short_Maturity_Debt_Against_Goodwill_Heavy_Equity
considered.hypothesis: Funding a goodwill-dominated equity base with debt that must be rolled over within the year creates refinancing risk against assets that cannot secure new lending; when credit conditions tighten these firms are forced to impair, dilute, or fire-sale.
considered.reasoning: The archive tested debt *issuance* against intangible intensity (weak on both metrics), but never the maturity structure of existing debt, which is the dimension that actually determines rollover exposure and is not an investment-rate or profitability sort that FF5 can span. Both legs are stock ratios reported by essentially all firms, so coverage should sit near the archive maximum and the portfolio composition should be stable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity_Added_Without_Staffing_Low_Margin
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(MIN(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), SUB(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), GROWTH(emp, 1)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that expands gross plant faster than it expands its workforce is building capacity it has not staffed to operate; at low-margin firms this unstaffed capacity is a fixed-cost commitment made without the rents to support it.
considered.reasoning: The MIN operator repairs the exact defect the critic identified — the score can only be high when plant growth is itself high *and* exceeds employment growth, so pure downsizing firms (falling headcount, flat plant) can no longer reach the top of the ranking. This makes the leg an unambiguous over-building measure rather than a restructuring proxy, and it is distinct from the archive's employment-minus-sales-growth leg because the benchmark is physical capacity rather than output.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Thin_Cash_Coverage_Of_Operating_Costs_With_Soft_Assets
considered.hypothesis: What matters for a soft-asset firm is not the direction of its cash balance but how many months of operating cost that balance covers: a firm with thin cash relative to its cost base and no pledgeable assets has no way to fund a bad year except dilution or asset write-offs.
considered.reasoning: The critic is right that a monotone denominator swap cannot change a rank-based slope, so this abandons the change-in-cash formulation entirely and substitutes a *level* state — cash runway measured against the operating cost base — which is a different economic quantity from the flow drain already evaluated. The interaction is then genuinely conditional: runway is only binding when the remaining assets cannot be pledged, which is precisely what the intangible share measures.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Capital_Being_Validated_In_Real_Time
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(revt, 1), GROWTH(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), 1))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))))
considered.hypothesis: The flagship result says soft capital that fails to produce output is overpriced; the symmetric and untested claim is that soft capital which is *demonstrably* producing more output per year — revenue growing faster than the capital base — is underpriced, because investors discount intangible-heavy balance sheets indiscriminately.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the mechanical merger of two evaluated long-side signals with a new economic claim: it is the *improvement* in capital productivity, not its level, that identifies which intangible-heavy firms deserve their carrying values, and the conditioning direction (high soft-asset share) is the opposite of every prior negative signal, so the result is not predictable from the parents. Both legs are near-universally reported and the growth differential is scale-free, giving stable cross-sectional ranking.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Roll_Up_Failing_To_Lift_Labor_Productivity
considered.hypothesis: The standard justification for a serial acquisition program is that combining organizations raises output per employee; a three-year acquisition wave followed by flat or falling revenue per worker is direct evidence that the promised synergies never arrived.
considered.reasoning: Measuring labor productivity as a three-year *within-firm growth rate* rather than a level removes the industry determination the critic flagged, since each firm is benchmarked against its own pre-acquisition productivity rather than against firms with different vertical integration. Matching the horizon of the productivity test to the horizon of the acquisition program makes this an integration-failure test rather than a conditioner swap on the flagship, and it differs from the archive's acquisition-wave signal by using output per worker instead of a profitability position.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Investment_In_Place_Of_Hard_Investment
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)), capx), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent)))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that spends more on buying companies and intangible assets than on its own plant is substituting purchased capital for organic capital; at firms whose existing capital already generates little revenue, that substitution is an admission that reinvestment in the core business is not worth making.
considered.reasoning: `Soft_Investment_Drift_Versus_Installed_Mix` worked on both metrics (fmb −3.07, alpha −2.2%, Sharpe −0.37) but its share-of-flow denominator can approach or cross zero when intangibles amortize, so this expresses the same substitution economics as a difference of two intensities over a strictly positive capital base — a stable, sign-preserving construction. This isolates a single measurement choice on a mechanism already shown to carry information, which is the appropriate use of a near-variant this late in the search.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Capital_Base_Without_Cash_Gross_Profit
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Purchased intangible capital is validated only by profit that converts to cash; a soft-asset-heavy firm whose gross profit is being consumed by inventory accumulation has accounting profitability without cash generation, and the carrying value of its intangibles is correspondingly less defensible.
considered.reasoning: This asks a substantive economic question about the archive's flagship — does its power run through profitability per se, or through profitability that actually converts into cash — by deducting the inventory investment that absorbs gross profit, which also brings an investment-theme variable inside the conditioner rather than leaving it purely an accounting margin. If the cash-adjusted version strengthens the result it identifies the conversion channel; if it does not, the flagship is a pure margin effect and the final generation should stop refining it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash_Position_At_Own_Five_Year_Low_With_Soft_Assets
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose cash relative to its own sales base sits at the bottom of its five-year range has exhausted the buffer it normally operates with; when its remaining assets are unpledgeable intangibles, that depletion cannot be reversed by borrowing against collateral.
considered.reasoning: This changes exactly one thing relative to `Thin_Cash_Coverage_Of_Operating_Costs_With_Soft_Assets` — the liquidity leg becomes a within-firm historical position rather than a cross-sectional level — so the result cleanly identifies whether the flat FMB slope alongside a −6.6% alpha came from permanently cash-rich business models occupying one extreme of the cross-sectional ranking. Benchmarking each firm against itself is also not the net-leverage/distress dimension, since a structurally cash-poor but stable firm scores neutrally.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Short_Term_Debt_Load_With_Goodwill_Heavy_Revenue_Base
considered.hypothesis: Carrying a large stock of debt due within the year is a genuine refinancing burden only in proportion to firm size, and it becomes dangerous when a large part of the asset base is goodwill rather than revenue-producing collateral, because lenders reprice or withdraw and the equity absorbs the adjustment.
considered.reasoning: Scale is retained by keeping the archive's original `dlc/at` leg untouched, so this makes exactly one change to `Short_Maturity_Debt_Against_Goodwill_Heavy_Equity`: replacing the `gdwl/ceq` conditioner, whose near-zero and negative denominators inverted the ranking for the most fragile firms, with goodwill per dollar of revenue, which is monotone and always well defined. That isolation makes the −4.7% alpha with a +0.23 slope interpretable — if the slope turns negative, the denominator pathology was the cause.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Fully_Depreciated_Plant_Still_Earning_Rents
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ppent, ppegt))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm operating largely written-down plant that still generates high gross profit per dollar of remaining book capital holds productive capacity whose economic value far exceeds its carrying value; because book-based valuation understates these assets, such firms are systematically underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This drops the issuance leg the critic identified as a published anomaly and replaces it with asset vintage — a construct the archive has used only on the short side — while switching the validating measure from revenue turnover to gross profit per unit of capital, so neither component repeats a previously mined pairing. The economics are also specific rather than generic: old assets earning rents means the depreciation schedule, not the business, is what makes the firm look capital-light.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Acquiring_When_Own_Labor_Productivity_Is_Depressed
considered.hypothesis: Managers buy revenue when their own organization has stopped producing it: purchasing companies and intangibles while output per employee sits at the bottom of its five-year range is a defensive deal made from operational weakness, and such deals disappoint.
considered.reasoning: The accounting linkage is broken because the conditioner no longer contains the capital base that acquisitions mechanically inflate — acquisitions add sales and employees roughly in proportion, so they do not push revenue per worker toward a trough by construction. Benchmarking labor productivity within the firm's own history also removes the industry determination that makes raw sales-per-employee unusable, and the timing framing (state *before* the deal) distinguishes this from the archive's post-acquisition disappointment signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Unverifiable_Young_Capital_Without_Cash_Profit
considered.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0))), RATIO(ppent, ppegt)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Capital is least trustworthy when it is both soft (purchased intangibles rather than plant) and young (recently installed, not yet proven); when such a capital base fails to generate cash-converted gross profit, the carrying value rests entirely on management projections and returns are low.
considered.reasoning: The archive's two best-performing legs — intangible share of capital (short side) and plant vintage (long side, entering with the opposite sign) — are two measurements of the same latent quantity, the verifiability and provenness of the asset base, so combining them as an equal-weighted rank sum sharpens a single economic axis rather than averaging unrelated anomalies. Conditioning on cash gross profit rather than accounting margin follows the generation-7 finding that cash conversion is the stronger validator, and all inputs are near-universally reported.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net_Short_Term_Funding_Gap_With_Goodwill_Heavy_Revenue
considered.hypothesis: What determines refinancing exposure is the shortfall between debt coming due and cash on hand; when that gap is positive and the asset base backing it is goodwill rather than revenue-producing collateral, the firm must refinance on worse terms and the equity bears the repricing.
considered.reasoning: The fragility family has twice delivered ~−4.7% alpha with a flat FMB slope because each attempt used a leg that is non-monotone across the cross-section — cash-rich firms sit at one extreme of `che/cogs`, and debt-free firms at one extreme of `dlc/at` — whereas netting the two into a single signed funding gap orders firms continuously from net-lender to net-borrower. This is the specific measurement repair the diagnosis calls for, not another conditioner swap.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Investment_Drift_With_Floored_Denominator
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)), MAX(ADD(capx, ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1))), capx)), RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent)))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose marginal investment dollar is softer than its installed asset mix is drifting out of its core business, and that drift is punished where the existing capital already generates little revenue.
considered.reasoning: The parent drift signal worked on both metrics (fmb −3.07, alpha −2.2%, Sharpe −0.37) but its denominator could approach zero when intangibles amortize; my generation-7 replacement removed the instability by also dropping the installed-mix benchmark and lost the entire slope (−0.30), proving the benchmark carried the information. Flooring the denominator at capex preserves the benchmark while eliminating the sign flips — the minimal fix that separates measurement noise from economics.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Goodwill_Share_Of_Capital_Without_Cash_Profit
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Within the intangible base, goodwill is the component with no identifiable underlying asset and no contractual cash flows; if the soft-capital effect is really about unverifiability, restricting the numerator to goodwill while holding the full capital base in the denominator should concentrate the result.
considered.reasoning: This decomposes the archive's best signal along the one dimension that distinguishes purchased-but-identifiable intangibles (patents, customer lists, licences, which amortize on schedules tied to contracts) from pure acquisition premium, a question the archive has never been able to answer because earlier attempts changed the denominator at the same time. Holding the denominator fixed at total capital makes this a clean numerator decomposition whose outcome tells the final generation which component to build on.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Capital_With_Profit_Absorbed_By_Inventory
considered.hypothesis: An intangible-heavy firm whose reported profit is being consumed by inventory accumulation is generating paper earnings while its cash goes into unsold goods; the combination of unverifiable capital and non-converting profit is where impairment and disappointment concentrate.
considered.reasoning: The critic is right that averaging DELTA(invt, 1) telescopes the accrual adjustment into irrelevance, so this abandons smoothing and instead promotes the accrual term itself to a standalone leg, making the test unambiguous — it contains no profitability level at all and therefore cannot collapse into gross-profitability-on-assets. Both components have been individually validated in the archive (soft-capital share and inventory buildup) but never paired, so the result speaks directly to whether unverifiable capital and non-converting profit compound.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Written_Down_Plant_With_High_Cash_Margin
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ppent, ppegt))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), sale)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm operating heavily depreciated plant while earning a high cash-converted margin on every sales dollar is harvesting rents from capacity that its balance sheet no longer reflects; because book capital understates the productive asset, the market underprices the durable cash stream.
considered.reasoning: The mechanical dependence the critic identified is eliminated because the conditioner is now a margin scaled by sales, sharing no variable with the vintage leg, so the product tests the genuine interaction of asset age with pricing power rather than re-loading on low net PP&E twice. Retaining the cash adjustment keeps the generation-7 lesson that cash-converted profit is the more reliable validator, while the sales denominator makes the conditioner comparable across capital intensities.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Capital_Unprofitable_And_Draining_Cash
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The terminal state for an intangible-heavy firm is one where the soft capital produces no cash profit and the cash buffer is simultaneously eroding: the write-down is coming and the firm will have to fund itself from weakness before it arrives.
considered.reasoning: The archive's two strongest and economically independent negative axes — soft-capital composition validated by cash profit (−4.9% alpha) and liquidity drain (−4.2% alpha, Sharpe −0.35) — have never been combined multiplicatively, and the generation-8 evidence shows that products sharpen while rank sums dilute, so the triple product should concentrate the short leg on firms failing on asset quality, profitability, and liquidity at once. All three components are near-universally reported, so coverage and portfolio stability should hold.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Old_Plant_And_No_Purchased_Intangibles
considered.hypothesis: The archetypal underpriced firm on this axis operates written-down physical capacity and buys no soft capital: its assets are real, proven, and carried below economic value, and management is not spending shareholder money on unverifiable purchases.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are independently validated long-side constructs — plant vintage produced the archive's largest slope (+5.04) and intangible run-off produced its best Sharpe (+0.41) — and unlike the diluted rank-sum composite they are combined multiplicatively and share no variable, so the interaction identifies firms that are simultaneously asset-proven and acquisition-disciplined. This is the strongest available consolidation of the positive side, where the archive's evidence has been thinnest.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Funding_Gap_With_Weak_Cash_Profit
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A positive net short-term funding gap is survivable for a firm generating cash profit and dangerous for one that is not; the interaction of refinancing need with cash-generation failure identifies firms that must refinance precisely when they cannot self-fund.
considered.reasoning: The fragility family has repeatedly delivered very large alphas (−4.7%, −4.6%, −6.3%) with flat FMB slopes because its conditioners — goodwill-to-equity, goodwill-to-revenue — are balance-sheet composition measures whose raw-return relationship is offset by value and profitability exposures; replacing the conditioner with cash profitability, the only conditioner in the archive that has consistently produced *both* a slope and an alpha, is the last untried way to align the two forms of evidence. If the slope remains flat with a large alpha, the conclusion is that this channel is genuinely factor-hedged rather than mismeasured.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt_Financed_Goodwill_Creation
considered.hypothesis: Goodwill created by a highly levered acquirer is the most fragile asset on any balance sheet: the premium was funded with fixed claims that must be serviced from the target's cash flows, so any shortfall forces impairment and equity value transfers to creditors.
considered.reasoning: The archive tested stock-financed goodwill creation and found the *opposite* sign (alpha +3.3%), which is consistent with equity-funded deals being cushioned by flexible claims; the debt-funded cell is the untested complement and the mechanism predicts the reverse. Both legs are near-universally defined, the leverage ratio is bounded between zero and one so it avoids the negative-equity pathology that broke earlier goodwill-to-equity constructs, and no variable is shared between the two legs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Asset_Base_With_Starved_Physical_Reinvestment
considered.hypothesis: Low physical reinvestment means opposite things depending on what the firm owns: for a hard-asset firm with rents it is harvesting written-down capacity, but for a firm whose balance sheet is dominated by purchased intangibles it means the entire asset base is decaying — soft capital that cannot be verified and hard capital that is not being maintained.
considered.reasoning: This is a genuinely new cell rather than a deflator change: the archive established that written-down plant earning rents is *underpriced* (fmb +5.04) and that soft capital is overpriced, and the natural test of whether both findings share one asset-quality mechanism is to combine low reinvestment with a soft rather than hard asset base, where the prediction reverses. The two legs share no variable, both are near-universally reported, and the reinvestment rate scaled by gross plant is a maintenance measure not previously paired with intangible intensity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft_Capital_With_Cost_Ratio_At_Own_Five_Year_High
considered.hypothesis: The soft-capital effect should be concentrated not in firms with structurally low margins but in firms whose own cost-to-sales ratio has just climbed to the top of its five-year range: that deterioration is the operational evidence that the acquired intangibles are losing their economic value and an impairment is approaching.
considered.reasoning: Every conditioner that has worked in this archive measures a cross-sectional *level* of profitability, which confounds business-model differences with deterioration; benchmarking the cost ratio against the firm's own five-year history isolates deterioration and asks a question the drift construct cannot — whether it is the turning point, not the level, that identifies mispriced soft capital. The bounded within-firm state avoids the persistence that neutralized the earlier peak-versus-drawdown design, and the conditioner is a cost-side measure never used in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: The conditional form (rank product of two positively-oriented components) is internally consistent with the negative expected sign and the inorganic-growth mechanism is a defensible sharpening of the asset-growth anomaly, though the un-COALESCEd `gdwl` will cut coverage and the large mass of zero goodwill changes will create heavy rank ties that blunt the interaction.

With `xrd`/`xad` COALESCEd to zero, a large fraction of the sample takes the exact value zero (destroying cross-sectional discrimination), and among the remainder the ratio rises mechanically whenever capex falls, so the signal is likely to re-express the well-known capex/investment-decline effect rather than any distinct intangible-reallocation mispricing.

The stated hypothesis is explicitly conditional ("the penalty is concentrated where R&D stock is absent") but the expression is an additive rank difference, which merely stacks two separately published anomalies (PP&E/asset growth negative, R&D-to-assets positive) and cannot test the interaction claimed.

This is a plain rank-difference blend of two long-established standalone anomalies — acquirer underperformance / acquisition intensity and the R&D-intensity premium — with no genuine interaction, so a strong result would be uninformative about the buy-versus-build mechanism it claims to isolate.

The multiplicative rank form correctly implements the stated conditional ("external finance is worst at intangible-poor firms"), the sign logic is internally consistent, coverage is protected by COALESCE, and the cross-theme conditioning is a substantive refinement of the net-external-financing anomaly rather than a repackaging of it — the main risk to diagnose later is that the intangible-intensity leg is largely an industry fixed effect.

The expression matches the conditional hypothesis and the sign is coherent, but the mechanism sits close to the documented result that the investment/asset-growth effect is concentrated among low-profitability, low-turnover firms, and the ratio's denominator (`intan + ppent`) goes near zero for asset-light firms, mislabeling them as hyper-productive.

This is largely a hybrid of two archive signals (Growth_With_Weak_Intangible_Productivity's productivity conditioner plus Plant_Buildout's ppegt growth leg) with a denominator tweak, and it introduces a mechanical coupling because ppegt enters both legs — high plant growth mechanically inflates the capital base and depresses revt/capital, so the two ranks are positively linked by construction rather than by economics.

A genuinely different conditioner (firm-specific organic top-line deceleration rather than an industry-proxy R&D dummy) with a coherent overpayment/impairment mechanism, though the author should note that acquisitions mechanically boost revt growth (so the interaction selects the residual set of acquirers still shrinking) and that low sales growth standalone is a value-like positive-return characteristic that may dampen the slope.

The reasoning explicitly claims to avoid ratio artifacts but the conditioner has the symmetric problem it disclaims — (xrd+xad)/sale falls whenever sales rise — and COALESCE-to-zero leaves the majority of non-reporting firms with an identically zero delta, creating a large rank mass point that makes the interaction degenerate to capex/ppent for much of the sample.

Labor as an investment margin is a genuinely distinct channel from the archive's capital/financing legs and is plausibly less spanned by CMA, though the reviewer should recognize that the hiring-rate anomaly is itself well documented and that zero-R&D firms all tie at the conditioner's extreme, so the signal effectively becomes employment growth within the non-innovator subsample.

This is an industry-neutralized re-run of the archive's Plant_Buildout_Without_Knowledge_Capital with a near-identical intangible leg — a standard robustness transformation rather than a new mechanism, and double-standardizing both legs will mostly shrink the spread rather than reveal a different economic effect.

The tangible-share leg equals exactly 1.0 for every firm not reporting xrd or xad, so the multiplicative form collapses to total capex/at ranked within the non-innovator subsample — i.e., a repackaging of the well-known capex/investment anomaly conditioned on a reporting dummy, which is close in spirit to the archive's tangible-buildout family.

This is a near-duplicate of the archive's Acquired_Intangible_Heavy_Base_Low_Gross_Profitability — in Compustat INTAN already contains GDWL, so dropping the (redundantly double-counted) intan term changes the composition ratio only marginally and will produce a signal highly correlated with the existing −4.7% alpha rather than a genuinely new test.

Multiplying two same-signed ranks of two of the most heavily published anomalies (R&D intensity/capitalized R&D stock and Novy-Marx gross profitability) yields a composite dominated by their main effects rather than a genuine interaction, and it reintroduces exactly the zero-R&D mass-at-the-bottom problem the other proposals in this batch criticize.

The working-capital investment margin is untouched by the archive and the gross-margin conditioner is economically motivated and internally consistent with the negative sign, though the reviewer should verify incremental power over the well-known Thomas–Zhang inventory-change anomaly that will dominate the first leg.

The diagnosis (unbounded growth rate producing tail-driven alpha with a flat FMB slope) is sound and the bounded within-firm conditioner is a substantive fix, but TS_RANK of the raw R&D *level* is confounded by firm size and nominal drift — a shrinking firm mechanically sits at its five-year low — so an intensity-scaled version (xrd/sale) would be the cleaner test, and coverage will remain thin.

Replacing R&D-per-worker with gross-profit-per-worker is a defensible, coverage-improving fix for the tied-at-zero conditioner that plausibly converts portfolio evidence into cross-sectional evidence, but it is a close relative of the archive signal and now stacks two known effects (hiring-rate anomaly and labor productivity/gross profitability), so the incremental content over the existing −3.3% alpha must be demonstrated.

Conditioning cumulative acquisition intensity on the firm's own five-year profitability position is a genuinely new dynamic ex-post-validation channel distinct from the archive's contemporaneous acquirer sorts, internally consistent in sign, and the bounded state-variable conditioner is a principled response to the unstable TREND-based versions — the main risk being that within-firm profitability troughs also proxy for mean-reverting distress.

The construct is internally consistent but is essentially the product of the two canonical FF5 legs — capex-to-assets (CMA/investment anomaly) and low gross profitability (RMW/Novy-Marx) — so it is close to the textbook q-theory investment×profitability interaction and its long-short alpha is the most likely of the batch to be mechanically spanned by the very factor model used to evaluate it.

Net-to-gross PP&E as a bounded stock proxy for recent capital-cycle vintage is a genuinely different investment measurement from the archive's flow and growth constructs, the conditioning logic and sign are coherent, and the main risk (industry variation in depreciation policy driving the vintage ratio) is a diagnosable rather than fatal issue.

With the identical conditioner and a near-identical economic story, this is largely a flow restatement of the archive's best performer (Acquired_Intangible_Heavy_Base_Low_Gross_Profitability), and the investment leg double-counts the same event since acquisitions mechanically generate the DELTA(intan) they are added to.

Employment growth net of sales growth is a rediscovery of Abarbanell–Bushee's labor-force-efficiency fundamental signal, but the diagnostic motivation (stripping the cyclical/size component that plausibly broke the archive's hiring-signal FMB slopes) is sound and the conditional overlay is a legitimate incremental test rather than a cosmetic tweak.

The capital-productivity idea is fresh, but placing three-year cumulative capex in the denominator makes the ratio explode and change sign for low-capex firms, so the cross-sectional ranking will be driven by 1/capex noise (i.e., asset-light firms) rather than by unproductive investment, and the intangible-composition leg substantially overlaps an existing archive conditioner.

This is the equity-issuance anomaly interacted with hard-to-value/intangible intensity — a well-documented published combination — and its conditioning direction directly contradicts the archive's Externally_Financed_Tangible_Buildout result (issuance penalty concentrated in *low*-intangible firms), so the proposal is largely a sign-flipped rerun of an already-evaluated cell without addressing why that evidence points the other way.

This is the archive flagship (intangible-heavy base × low gross profitability, fmb −4.33 / alpha −4.7%) with an asset-growth rank bolted on, so it is largely a cosmetic extension of an already-tested signal and its incremental content — asset growth conditioned on profitability — is the well-published q-theory investment×profitability interaction.

The noise-diversification motive is legitimate, but the nested SUMRANK silently weights inventory growth 1/2 versus labor and capex 1/4 each, contradicting the stated equal "pooling" of three margins, and the resulting construct is close to a generic composite-investment × profitability sort already spanned by CMA/RMW.

Pooling a margin and a turnover conditioner is a coherent DuPont-style idea, but it holds the flagship's composition leg fixed and merely swaps in a second, mechanically overlapping denominator (intan+ppent appears in both legs), making it a variant rather than a substantively new mechanism.

The proposal correctly diagnoses why the three-year capex signal had a flat FMB slope (skewed asset-scaled dollar legs) and replaces it with a scale-free difference of long-horizon growth rates in a distinct input (plant vs. labor), giving a testable and economically coherent capacity-utilization story rather than a relabeling.

Industry-standardizing one leg of the archive's best signal is a useful robustness diagnostic but is exactly the kind of cosmetic variant the objective warns against, and it duplicates the IND_ADJ approach already tried in the capex/peer-margin signal.

Low/negative investment growth combined with high gross profitability per unit of capital is essentially a long CMA×RMW position, so it is a direct rediscovery of two of the very factors the alpha is measured against and should mechanically deliver little abnormal return.

This is an equal-weight blend of two already-evaluated archive signals (Acquired_Intangible_Heavy_Base_Low_Gross_Profitability and Liquidity_Drain_Without_Margin_Cushion) sharing the identical gross-profitability conditioner, so it will almost mechanically land between their existing statistics and teach nothing new about the mechanism.

Internally consistent and a defensible economic reframing of the run-off story, but the two legs are mechanically linked (a firm not buying intangibles is by construction spending less cash), so the "conditional" structure risks being a near-degenerate restatement of a single non-acquisition state rather than an independent interaction.

The bounded revenue-drawdown conditioner is well-motivated by the prior FMB evidence and the sign logic is coherent, but this is now the fourth RANK(capx/ppent) × RANK(conditioner) construct in the archive and it overlaps materially with Three_Year_Capex_Program_With_No_Revenue_Response, so the incremental information is limited to whether a drawdown level beats a revenue change.

A genuinely unexplored second-moment construct with a coherent governance/monitoring rationale and a sign that matches the expression's natural direction; the main risk to diagnose is that capex-rate volatility proxies for firm size, age, and idiosyncratic volatility rather than allocation discipline.

The inventory-growth-minus-sales-growth leg is close to the published inventory-growth anomaly and the conditioner is essentially DuPont asset turnover, so novelty rests entirely on the interaction, but the leg itself is new to this archive and the design question (is the long side a general capital-discipline effect?) is legitimate.

This is an explicitly cosmetic variant of Labor_Bloat_Relative_To_Output_Low_Margin with only the conditioner swapped, and since gross-profit-to-assets and revenue-to-capital are highly correlated cross-sectionally, the result is very likely to replicate the existing signal without isolating anything economically new.

The flow-versus-stock composition gap is a genuinely new within-firm construct not present in the archive, but the soft-investment share has a denominator (capx + aqc + Δintan) that can approach or cross zero when intangibles amortize down, producing sign flips and unstable ranks that could easily dominate the economics, so it should be winsorized or floored before testing.

The expression is high whenever headcount falls sharply — i.e., for restructuring/downsizing firms — which is the opposite of the "substituting fixed capital for labor and raising operating leverage" story, and once decomposed it is close to the archive's growth-minus-employment-growth family paired with the same NEG(GP/AT) conditioner.

The stated diagnosis is wrong — RANK is invariant to monotone transforms so right-skew in intan/sale cannot explain the weak slope, and the zero mass in intangibles produces identical ties under the bounded share — leaving this as a cosmetic denominator swap on Liquidity_Drain_At_Soft_Asset_Firms.

This is a mechanical equal-weight merger of two already-evaluated signals sharing the identical conditioner; it may modestly improve reliability but adds no new economic content and its result is largely predictable from the two parents.

Debt maturity structure is a legitimately untested dimension here with a coherent rollover-risk mechanism, but scaling goodwill by ceq means the most fragile firms (negative or near-zero book equity) receive large negative or explosive values that invert the intended ranking, so the conditioner should be scaled by assets or the sample cleaned of ceq ≤ 0.

This is a single-conditioner swap on the archive's flagship Acquired_Intangible_Heavy_Base_Low_Gross_Profitability, and the substituted leg (raw, non-industry-adjusted sales per employee) is one of the most industry-determined ratios in accounting data, so the product will largely sort on industry rather than on failed synergy realization.

This is a near-duplicate of the archive's `Thin_Cash_Coverage_Of_Operating_Costs_With_Soft_Assets` with the same intangible-share conditioner and a liquidity leg that changes two things at once (netting `dlc` and rescaling to sales), so a shift in results cannot be attributed to the stated non-monotonicity diagnosis, and the first leg is largely a restatement of the well-known net-leverage/distress dimension.

The critique of the `gdwl/ceq` denominator is legitimate and the fix is sensible, but replacing `dlc/at` with the maturity *share* `dlc/(dlc+dltt)` discards scale entirely — a firm with trivial total debt that happens to be short-dated ranks as maximally rollover-exposed — which contradicts the hypothesis that the equity absorbs a refinancing repricing.

The first leg is essentially the published net-external-financing / composite-issuance anomaly (Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan, Daniel-Titman) and the `revt/(intan+ppent)` conditioner has already been mined twice in the archive with positive results, so a strong outcome would most likely reflect the issuance effect plus a re-used conditioner rather than a genuinely new interaction.

A defensible stability-motivated re-specification of a signal that already worked on both metrics, though it quietly drops the installed-mix benchmark that made the parent distinctive — reducing it to a soft-minus-hard investment intensity — and the denominator can still approach zero for asset-light firms.

The margin-versus-cash-conversion question is a substantive diagnostic rather than a cosmetic tweak, but the conditioner is a partial rediscovery of cash-based operating profitability (Ball et al. 2016) implemented with an arbitrary and incomplete accrual adjustment that deducts inventory alone while ignoring receivables and payables.

The two legs are mechanically linked — buying intangibles inflates the `intan+ppent` denominator and therefore pushes the firm's own five-year `revt/(intan+ppent)` rank toward its trough by construction — so the interaction will partly reflect an accounting identity rather than the claimed timing decision, and the design otherwise closely echoes `Acquisition_Wave_Followed_By_Profitability_Trough`.

The composite is directionally consistent with both parent results and not a known published anomaly, but the claim that intangible share and net/gross PP&E measure one latent "verifiability" axis is weak — for intangible-heavy firms ppent/ppegt is computed on a tiny plant base and is mostly noise — so the SUMRANK may simply dilute the stronger intangible-share leg rather than sharpen it.

This is a one-parameter smoothing of the archive's existing best signal, and worse, MA of DELTA(invt,1) telescopes to (invt_t − invt_{t−3})/3, which shrinks the inventory adjustment toward negligible size and effectively reverts the conditioner to plain gross-profitability-on-assets (Novy-Marx), so the test cannot distinguish "persistent cash-conversion failure" from simply dropping the accrual adjustment.

Beyond being a single-input substitution on an already-tested construct, both legs share ppent — low net PP&E simultaneously raises NEG(ppent/ppegt) and the profit-per-capital ratio — so the product largely re-loads on the same variable rather than testing a genuine interaction, and the "cash rents" refinement will not separate that mechanical dependence from the hypothesized hidden-capacity effect.

The diagnosis is correct and specific — the fragility family's flat FMB slopes plausibly stem from non-monotone one-sided legs — and netting cash against current debt into a signed funding gap is a substantive measurement repair rather than a conditioner swap, though the resulting leg overlaps materially with known net-leverage and cash-holdings effects and should be checked against a plain net-debt control.

The floor does what is claimed — the denominator can no longer fall below capx when intangibles amortize, removing sign flips — and the failed generation-7 variant justifies preserving the installed-mix benchmark, but this remains a numerical-stability tweak on an already-working signal and it still degenerates for near-zero-capex firms.

Holding the denominator fixed while restricting the numerator to goodwill is a legitimate and previously unanswered decomposition, but the informational gain is limited because Compustat intan typically subsumes gdwl and the gen-1 signal already used (gdwl+intan)/(ppent+gdwl+intan) with a near-identical conditioner, so the two constructs will be highly correlated and the "which component" verdict may be indeterminate.

The triple rank product is a legitimate untested stack of two archive winners, but the two parents already share the (near-identical) low-profitability leg, so the marginal information comes almost entirely from the cash-drain term, and triple products of ranks tend to concentrate mass in a few extreme names and destabilize portfolio composition — accept, but expect incremental rather than additive gains.

This is the archive's Soft_Capital_Base_Without_Cash_Profit with the conditioner's deflator changed from `at` to `sale` and nothing else — a textbook cosmetic variant that the research objective explicitly warns against, and the deflator question could be settled by a diagnostic on the existing signal rather than a new proposal.

A genuinely new pairing of two independently validated long-side legs with no shared variable, though it is exposed to rediscovery risk on both sides (low `ppent/ppegt` is essentially the known asset-age/vintage effect and low Δintan is a slice of the asset-growth anomaly), and dropping the profitability leg removes the very term that distinguished "written-down but still earning rents" from "old plant in a dying business."

Internally consistent and motivated by a real diagnosis (flat slopes from balance-sheet-composition conditioners), but the resulting construct is close to "financial distress × low gross profitability," a combination well covered by the published distress and profitability literatures, so novelty is thin even if the evidence turns out strong.

Sign and mechanism are coherent, the legs share no variable, and it is a well-motivated complement to the archive's contrarian stock-financed result — but the reasoning's claim that `dltt/(ceq+dltt)` is bounded in [0,1] is false for negative-book-equity firms, exactly the distressed tail the signal is meant to capture, so the leverage leg needs a floor or winsorization before the result can be trusted.

The drift construct has already been tested twice (generations 6 and 8) and this changes only the conditioner to a quantity highly correlated with the incumbent revenue-turnover conditioner, making it a third pass at the same signal rather than a substantively different mechanism.
